talo...@yahoo.ca (Geoff) wrote in message

> So how is [play to win] enforced lsj? My prey takes one look at his preys

> vampire and offers a tablesplit. What is the judge supposed to do?

It is enforced like any other rule - violations of the rule are noted
and not allowed. If a violation is brought to the judge's attention
after the fact, then the game is rewound to the point of the violation
and the violation is removed. If a player refuses to play to win (or
refuses to follow any of the rest of the body of rules), then that
player should be removed (and game state corrected).

> What if he states he cannot win (or believes that at least) and
> therefore wants to maximize his vps with a split?

If he can convince the judge that, based on game state, he cannot win,
then he is free to procede with his not winning in whatever (legal)
manner he chooses. It is quite difficult to "take one look at his
preys vampire" in the early part of a game and deduce that one cannot
win, however.

What the player believes is of no relevance. It is what the judge
believes that matters when it comes to a player's chances of winning.

There are a number of reasons.

One: People play with Wakes. Tapped almost never equals "cannot block",
and also almost never equals "cannot defend". Most decks are designed
to tap out every turn or leave a single vampire untapped, no more.
Those that aren't are frequently intercept decks.

Two: If you are an intercept/combat deck, you typically bleed very
slowly; blocking your prey's action will let you put his vampire in
torpor. From then forward, you can block all his rescue actions,
putting more vampires in torpor. Eventually he has no ready minions,
and you can neither Wake nor Deflect with a minion in torpor. Much more
reliable than hoping he doesn't have a Wake.

Three: If your prey is a stealth/bleed deck, and your grandprey cannot
block the stealthy actions, but you can. It is in your best interest to
prevent your grandprey from being ousted, thus causing your prey to gain
6 pool, a VP, and make him much harder to oust.

I can keep going, but really, those three say enough.

Why wouldn't someone try to win?

I see three general possibilities. The first being players who don't care
about the game from the standpoint of winning and losing - random game
elements. How do you deal with these people? You hope they don't play
tournaments (or at all, depending upon what you want from the game). You
certainly don't expect them in the finals. Except, it is possible that someone
engineered getting the player in the finals hoping to take advantage of their
play style. Not likely. Anyway, a play to win rule isn't likely to impact
these players sufficiently since they were already playing to screw up the game
by not caring about trying to win in the first place. You can try to punish
them. You run into the problem of how easy it is to justify bad play.

Second group - colluders. I see no need for a play to win rule to deal with
this group. Collusion is illegal per other rules.

Third group - maximizing tournament position-ers. I don't see any problem
here. These players want to win, they are even trying to win what should
obviously be the goal - the tournament - by manipulating games during the
prelims.

The only time I can see worrying about the legality of whether someone is
playing to win is when there's a suspicion of behavior that is already illegal
per other rules - collusion, player intimidation, etc. In the case of random
game elements, the much simpler way to go is likely to just ban them from
future events (for instance, a two tournament ban). So, a specific play to win
rule, besides being a royal bitch to enforce, shouldn't be necessary.

whether I'm better than you? There's no way to tell, of course; we

influence the outcome of the next.

No, the flaw in the BCS is that it exists, period.

An elimination bracket is the only way to guarantee that every team
tries its hardest to win (losing never helps you), and that there is a
reasonably good chance that the best team has won. Occasionally there
will exist the A beats B beats C beats A circle, but it's pretty rare.

benefit; the prey gets no pressure or less pressure for at least one
turn, maybe more. For this play to be legal, the prey must only have a
decent reason to believe that his predator is an immediate threat to
him. It's usually patently obvious.

I find this line of argument very unsettling. To be honest, I'm
not sure I agree with even the spirit of the "Play to Win" rule.
In poker tournaments, where real money is on the line, generally,
any kind of deal you want to make with the other players is legal.

Here are my thoughts:

1) You're requiring the judge to be as competent a player, possibly
much more so, than the players themselves. So basically, to enforce
the "Play to Win" rule, the Judge has to play the player's deck,
make judgement calls about the best play and then penalize the player
for not making them? That sounds pretty sketchy to me. Furthermore,
the Judge / TO has to be aware of every deck strategy out there and
how they play in all situations? Then you add on the table psychology?
That sounds to me like as a judge you'd have to sit there and do
nothing but watch the game, on top of being a better player than anyone
else at the table to be confident enough to EXPEL A PLAYER for not
playing the way you expect them to? I'll tell you right now that as
a judge and tournament organizer, I'd rather chuck the whole rule and
let players make any kind of deal openly than have to do that.

2) What about the fact that a player might be openly accepting a deal,
with the intention of backstabbing the player later to increase their
chances of winning? Case in point : suppose
Arika S&B promises Rush/Grapple to split the table in exchange for
not rushing Arika. Several turns later, Arika backstabs R/G and bleeds
them out. As a judge, if you interfered with that play based on your
interpretation of the rule, you would have prevented IMO a very good
psychological/backstab play. If you don't like that example, I'm sure
there are others you can come up with.

3) I realize Collusion could be a problem in a multiplayer game, and
the "Play to Win" rule prevents that. But if that's the case, why
not make the rule "No Collusion" rather than "Play to Win"? IMHO
that represents the spirit of the rules better, and if the judge has
to play detective to enforce the rule (which I think that he or she
will have to do) sniffing out collusion sounds fairer and more even
handed than forcing people to play their decks a certain way. Certainly
this could be fleshed out more..

Cheers,

Howdy Tim,

> I find this line of argument very unsettling. To be honest, I'm
> not sure I agree with even the spirit of the "Play to Win" rule.

So you'd be down with the 'players may play to win, to lose, to make
others win, to make others lose, or to whatever alternate victory
conditions they so desire' alteration to the Object of the Game I
proposed? If not, what would you replace it with?

> In poker tournaments, where real money is on the line, generally,
> any kind of deal you want to make with the other players is legal.

Including collusive ones? Boy, that must make for pointless games.

> Here are my thoughts:
>
> 1) You're requiring the judge to be as competent a player, possibly
> much more so, than the players themselves. So basically, to enforce
> the "Play to Win" rule, the Judge has to play the player's deck,
> make judgement calls about the best play and then penalize the player
> for not making them?

See, this wildly misconstrues 'play to win'. The judge has no
responsibility to insure players are making the _best_ plays possible.
It's only in their purview to prevent plays that are illegal.
There's a world of difference between the two. I'll certainly grant
that there's less difference between stupid play and illegal play, but
in no way grant that preventing illegal play in any way requires
enforcing optimal play.

Any path toward winning is an acceptable path. And even some paths
that don't head towards winning are legal, presuming that the player
attempting the path _believes_ the path to be winning, though this is
where things get furrier. (If he believes it in the face of available
evidence to the contrary - i.e. he's delusional - then the judge's
responsibilities get tricky. Incompetent players are always tricky to
handle, though. If he just doesn't know that the move is losing,
well, he's still playing to win.) What's not acceptable is
deliberately playing not to win, which is rightly labelled
'unsportsmanlike'.

> 2) What about the fact that a player might be openly accepting a deal,
> with the intention of backstabbing the player later to increase their
> chances of winning? Case in point : suppose
> Arika S&B promises Rush/Grapple to split the table in exchange for
> not rushing Arika. Several turns later, Arika backstabs R/G and bleeds
> them out. As a judge, if you interfered with that play based on your
> interpretation of the rule, you would have prevented IMO a very good
> psychological/backstab play. If you don't like that example, I'm sure
> there are others you can come up with.

How precisely it was illegal has not been specified here, but
presumably is was the losing end of a 3/2 split? Which would make the
Arika deck the predator of the Rush? Why would the Rush player make
such a deal, especially if it allowed the Arika deck to build enough
resources to oust it so quickly? Is he expecting the deal to be
broken? He should, as it looks illegal _and_ stupid, as Arika decks
shouldn't have much trouble with Rush, between S:CE, prevent _and_
Obedience. Generalizing, though, why shouldn't any two decks sitting
down next to each other cut such a deal, if not for 'play to win'?

Wouldn't other players at the table be right to object to having the
game apparently decided in haphazard fashion by a lame deal? Would
they be right to start suspecting collusion? Why play it out at that
point? Oh, because one of the dealmakers _might_ break the deal after
it was too late for the rest of the table to have any impact? This is
Diplomacy, not Jyhad. Discouraging this kind of dealmaking and
breaking is just fine by me.

> 3) I realize Collusion could be a problem in a multiplayer game, and
> the "Play to Win" rule prevents that. But if that's the case, why
> not make the rule "No Collusion" rather than "Play to Win"?

You need to review the relevant rules. Both 'play to win' and 'no
collusion' are separate sections of the V:EKN tournament rules. The
former is not a rule, per se, but a consequence of the 'sportsmanship'
rules as applied to the Object of the Game. And, of course, while
collusion involves not playing to win, not playing to win does not
necessarily involve collusion. The collusion rules are a necessary,
if almost entirely unenforceable, section of tournament rules.
(Unenforceable, as the only way to 'prove' collusion is to get an
admission from one or more of the players.) Collusion will generally
require unsportsmanlike play, however, and that play can and should be
prevented by the judge. Without the very basic tool of 'play to win'
that would be impossible.

Alex

expel someone for colluding. In poker, people often make deals because
they believe that there is a good chance that the game will be decided
by luck rather than skill, and they don't want to go through the motions.
I think there should be room for that in VTES as well. Suppose it comes
down to two players, 3-2, and the two players, acting in their own
best interest, decide to allow the 2VP player to withdraw? That seems like
it would violate the Play To Win rule, but I saw it happen at GenCon last
year, with no complaints - it saved time and both of the players agreed

all the time. The other players can (and do) try to persuade each other

fun of the game. So, it's illegal for a good player to try to make
a deal with a newbie player, trying to get into a heads up situation with
a player they know they can beat, after clearing the rest of the table?

same deal, not trying to get someone expelled from the tournament.

Now, going back to the example of the Newbie player who likes to rush
cross table and never gets a VP - There's a choice here. You can kick the
player out of the tournament. Or, you could let the experienced players
try to do some diplomacy and show that they really can make psychological
plays, by trying to manipulate the poor player. The poor player gets to
stay in the game, might even learn something, and the "good" players might
learn something too.

It must either be 3-0, 2-1, or 1-1-1. Taking each case individually:

legal (although silly, as extra VP determine finals seating order and
therefore you should always try to get as many as possible). The player

chooses.

player to withdraw, thus causing himself to win 3-2, this is legal from

play-to-win rule. If the player on the WRONG end of the 2-1 score is
trying to get out with only 2VP, I'd want to feel confident that he was
either actually in, or had reason to believe he was in, a hopeless
position, as he is giving up his chance at a Game Win. Often this is
true, but it is situationally dependent.

3) If the score is 1-1-1, then each player must attempt to oust the
other. Mutual withdrawal does not provide a Game Win (2-2-1). Timeouts
do not provide a Game Win (1.5-1.5-1). The only thing that will allow
each player to play for the win here is to attempt to oust the other

this situation; and conveniently, it only takes one person to decide he
wants to try to win to force the other person to do the same.

kick him out? I say no. If you're the kind of player who is can't
deal with the luck of the seating order and the suck up to a newbie
diplomacy that's required, I don't think there should be a rule to
bail you out. This player always plays the way he does, and I'm not

they were colluding to abuse the tournament and steal the prizes.

players believe that there's a good chance that luck rather than skill
will determine the outcome. I think this is fair since it reduces the
amount of luck and reduces the time it takes to finish the round, both
of which are good for the tournament. This could easily happen in VTES
with two players facing heads up and deciding to let one player withdraw.

to the "Play to Win" Rule.

it, not the judge. If I were a player at the table, I'd be kicking myself
for not trying to make a deal with the inexperienced player, not calling
over a judge.

>There's more to life then enforcing rules or playing to win. Making
>things enjoyable for all is way more important.

Out of context, this doesn't sound so bad. In the context of the current
discussion, this is ludicrous.

Rules exist to enable players to have fun playing the game. The goal of the
game exists to enable players to have fun playing the game. If people don't
like the game, then they should find something else to play. You know, like
tournaments [that would be a "clever" joke].

Which isn't necessarily that hard. It's entirely possible that the entire play
group wants to play some variant of the CCG that has more role-playing elements
or whatever. As long as everyone is on the same page, it doesn't matter what
you are doing or what the rules are.

But. When you get together people who aren't necessarily on the same page, you
must try to play to the only set of rules you can. Otherwise, might as well
not bother playing.

I once had a tendency to screw around in multiplayer CCGs. For two-player, it
mattered not at all since my opponent would just win easily, possibly why I
don't recall ever doing it with two-players. Anyway, a couple games around the
same time made me realize something(s). When someone isn't trying to win,
winning is meaningless. Now, maybe in a tournament, you can take heart in all
of the prizes you got that the random game elements didn't, though you are just
as likely to get annoyed by how someone else scored the better prizes because
the random game element decided to screw with you. In normal play, why was the
game played?

Led me to the concept of "good faith effort" (in CCGs). It's fine to not go
everything possible to try to win, to not build the best deck conceivable, and
whatever - you don't have to win. You must try to win. Now, this may sound
odd given my view on tournaments, but I just adapt it to tournaments by saying
that you must try to win the tournament rather than the game.

I sort of skimmed over an essential part of the argument, so I should get back
to it. Fun. Why don't we just have fun!?! Very simple problem with "fun".
It's personal. The rules define fun because nothing else can. Yes, the
*rules* define fun. I may know what someone finds fun, I may know what I find
fun, I may be able to guess what others find fun, but I'll never know for sure
what everyone I play with finds fun. That's what the rules are for.

Again, if you play with certain people exclusively, collectively you may have
decided that what you are doing is fun. You may also be playing a different
game, if a very similar one.

I should stop. But, there's something less philosophical I want to bring up.
Far too many players of CCGs I've run across are selfish. They don't care
whether anyone else has fun. They play to their own goals at the expense of
others and think nothing of it. So why not just stop playing with them?
That's what should be done, but it's hard when you have a small player base.
The long term move of fixing your group comes at the expense that you may never
get to the long term.
